COMPANION: It cites the independence paper and re-develops its method rather than using Theorem 1.1 as a lemma. Its bound χ ≤ C<sub>r</sub>Δ/log Δ, for maximum degree Δ, gives α ≥ n/χ, and deleting the vertices of degree above 2d then yields Theorem 1.1 without citing it. But it re-develops the method of §§2–5 (in its own words, "[22, Sections 2–5]"), so a flaw there would likely reach both. It is not an independent check.
WORLD: Our sources seat checked the paper's citations against the sources themselves: Ajtai–Erdős–Komlós–Szemerédi p. 314 (Equation (3), average valency, every fixed clique size, read from the rendered scan), Shearer's Corollary 2 (average degree), Alon's Theorem 1.1 and the remark after it, Davies' arXiv:2609.04654 (whose §3.3 potential is FG at unit parameters), Kleinberg–Tardos, Angel–Spinka, and Benjamini–Duminil-Copin–Kozma–Yadin. All match. Two primary sources, Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi 1980 and Shearer 1983, were paywalled and were checked only through secondary sources. Two wording notes: the order n log d/d is best possible in the sparse range (Ajtai–Erdős–Komlós–Szemerédi take t < n1/3), and Dhawan's "bounded numbers of cliques" grow with d. We found no claimed proof independent of OpenAI's argument, and no public objection to this one. The only technical engagement we found is Ross Kang's Zenodo note "Ode to the Ajtai–Erdős–Komlós–Szemerédi conjecture" (13 October). It adapts OpenAI's §§2–5 to the constant 2−18·n·log d/(rd) and reports no error, but it declares itself wholly AI-generated under Kang's curation and uses the same architecture, so it is not an independent check. Kaizhe Chen's arXiv:2610.15293 (11 October) already combines Theorem 1.1 with OpenAI's r(5,t) lower bound, which we have not refereed, to get r(4,t) = t³/(log t)2+o(1). Thomas Bloom's 8 October post lists #802 among OpenAI's claims and says the list is not an endorsement. Formal Conjectures added erdos_802 only on 20 October (PR #7165), marked research open, with no mention of OpenAI's claim. The community database still says open. The openai/math repository has issues disabled and pull-request conversations locked, so review cannot happen there; the open venue is the comment thread under Bloom's post. The paper has not been revised since the release.

SEATSUMMARY: ; the two on the mathematics logged eight exposition notes between them
READING: The main seat read §§1–6 line by line and found no gap. Two hostile AI referee seats on the mathematics, each told to refute and to quote what it objected to, found none either. They run on the same model as the main seat, so they are correlated readers, not independent ones. Seat O took §2 and §6. It re-derived every step and ran the multiplier construction of Lemma 2.2 literally in exact rational arithmetic, 3,708 times on K3-, K4- and K5-free graphs with ε down to 10⁻⁶, and no property ever failed; the tightest step, pi > ε/8, came within a factor 1.013. It checked each intermediate inequality of Lemma 2.3's proof on 540 instances and confirmed the identity in the first line of (6.3) exactly on 300 graphs, and (6.2) exactly given (2.1) and to 10⁻¹⁴ at 60 computed maximizers. It also reported that its own brute-force test of the cross-mass bound (2.5) could not have failed. On any graph small enough to compute, stationarity alone keeps the ratio below about log n/log log n, far under the constant; so the evidence for Lemma 2.3 is the hand check. Seat T took §§3–5. It re-derived every displayed identity and inequality with the printed constants, and checked the mechanical ones numerically. Five were checked beside a control built to fail: reversibility, the entropy-increment identity, the exact passage to the ordered triangle law, Lemma 5.2's E ℓ = Hj, and the fact that splitting never raises the best cross-mass constant. The density bound, the monotone entropies and the survival rule of Lemma 5.3 were checked without one. Seat L mapped the Lean to the paper. Seats O and T made eight exposition notes between them, and seats L and W two each, on the Lean and on wording. Three are worth repeating. Kuj is reversible because it is a polynomial in Pu; a product of reversible kernels need not be. The displayed iterate in the proof of Theorem 3.1 drops factors in [0, 1], which is valid as an inequality. And the remark that Lemma 2.3 is "the only consequence of extremality needed" should say global maximality. That last point is sharp, and the example is ours (seat O's, checked by hand by the main seat). On the triangle-free graph Km,k with m ≈ e3000 and k ≈ 3000e, the solution of (2.1) that is constant on each side puts weight about e−3000 on each vertex of the large side and about e−1 on each of the small side. It is not a maximizer: F is about 6,001 there, against e3000 for weight 1 on the large side. The two sides then weigh about 1 and 3,000, the cross mass between them is about 3,000, and at x = log 3000 the ratio in (2.5) is about 374.7, above 16·3² = 144, the paper's constant for triangle-free graphs (and above 16·4² = 256 too). The paper only ever uses global maximizers, and so does the Lean (IsOptimizer is the global-maximum predicate), so nothing breaks. The example shows that hypothesis cannot be weakened to a solution of (2.1).
